Project finance & ESIA · Nigeria

Spatial baselines for ESIAs, RAPs and compensation in Nigeria

Environmental and social impact assessments, resettlement action plans and compensation enumerations in Nigeria all start from the same question. What stood on this land, and on which date? We deliver dated, reviewed structure registers, settlement and land-cover baselines and estimated households as GIS layers and maps your consultancy, lender or project team can build on, and re-survey the footprint after the cut-off date.

Send us the project area See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

The dates that matter are the hardest to show

Every ESIA, RAP and compensation exercise turns on what was on the land on a given day. Site visits answer that on the day of the visit. Dated imagery answers it for the days in between.

“We need numbers before the field campaign.”

Enumerator teams, consultation schedules and the budget for a census all need a count and a map of the structures in the footprint before anyone goes to the field.

“New structures appeared after the cut-off date.”

Once a project is announced, building can follow. A dated register at the cut-off, and re-surveys after it, show which structures were there and which arrived later.

“The enumeration is disputed.”

Compensation enumerations on rights of way are contested structure by structure. A dated, reviewed record of what stood where gives both sides the same starting point.

“We can’t visit as often as the monitoring plan says.”

Lenders and independent monitors see a site a few times a year. Dated imagery between visits shows where land clearing, construction or settlement has moved on.

Who this is for

  • ESIA and RAP consultancies
  • Resettlement and social-performance teams
  • Lenders’ environmental and social advisers
  • Independent monitors and project implementation units
  • Land-acquisition and compensation teams
  • Valuers, as users of the structure inventory

The law

What the EIA Act and the land laws ask for

A summary of the public rules as of 26 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

EIA Act mandatory studies

The Environmental Impact Assessment Act (Decree No. 86 of 1992, Cap E12) lists projects for which a study is mandatory. For energy and linear projects they include:

  • oil and gas field development;
  • “off-shore pipelines in exceed of 50 kilometres”;
  • separation, processing, handling and storage facilities, and refineries;
  • product depots of 60,000 barrels or more within 3 km of homes, businesses or industry;
  • fossil-fuel steam power stations over 10 MW;
  • agricultural programmes that resettle 100 families or more.

Onshore pipelines are not a named item, so their category is settled under the 2021 EIA Procedures with the Federal Ministry of Environment.

Land, compensation and resettlement

Instrument What it provides
Land Use Act, s.28 Revocation for “overriding public interest”, which includes land for “mining purposes or oil pipelines”
Land Use Act, s.29 Compensation under the mining or petroleum law in those cases (s.29(2)); community compensation to the community, its chief or a fund (s.29(3)); buildings at replacement cost less depreciation (s.29(4))
Land Use Act, s.33 Resettlement may be offered instead of compensation for a residential building
Oil Pipelines Act, s.6 Notice before entering buildings or enclosed gardens on a pipeline survey, with compensation for damage
Petroleum Industry Act 2021, s.115 Compensation for land acquired for petroleum operations
IFC Performance Standard 5 The census, the asset inventory and the cut-off date on lender-financed projects

World Bank-financed projects in Nigeria, such as the DARES energy-access programme, apply the Bank’s own Environmental and Social Standard on land acquisition and resettlement.

For ESIA teams

The spatial baseline, as GIS layers and maps

An ESIA baseline needs to show what is around the project before it starts: settlements and structures, land cover and land use, flood-prone ground and terrain, and how all of it has been changing. We deliver each as a layer your team can load into its own GIS and map in its own report:

  • Structures in the footprint and in the rings around it that your study area sets, reviewed by a person, with categories where scoped;
  • Settlement growth trends, showing where built-up land has expanded year by year;
  • Land use and land cover: built-up land, cropland, bare ground, water and tree cover, from open datasets that are credited;
  • Terrain and flood exposure: steep and erosion-prone stretches and ground that has flooded in past satellite records;
  • Estimated households, with the assumptions stated, for consultation planning and to size the socio-economic survey;
  • Imagery history of the footprint: what was built, cleared or changed, and roughly when.

What a baseline layer is, and isn’t

The land-cover classes are generalised: it is not a cadastral, agricultural or ecological survey. Flood screening is not a hydraulic model. Households are estimates, not a census. Every layer names its source and date.

Resettlement and compensation

A dated record at the cut-off, then what arrived after it

At the cut-off date, we record the structures in the footprint from dated imagery, a drone survey or a satellite scene with a known capture date, never from undated basemap tiles. Each structure gets an ID, coordinates, a photo crop and, where scoped, a reviewer category that describes what the imagery shows. That register supports the census and asset inventory under IFC Performance Standard 5, and the compensation enumeration for a right of way under the Land Use Act.

After the cut-off, the footprint is re-surveyed on a schedule you agree with us. New structures are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, and each re-survey can be packaged as an evidence pack: the imagery, the registers and the maps with file fingerprints and an independent timestamp, to support legal and community processes.

Where the date comes from

The record reflects the imagery’s capture date. For a cut-off date, we look for dated scenes close to it and tell you what exists before you commit. A new satellite capture can be requested when the archive is too old; its date depends on satellite availability and weather, so it is never guaranteed.

For lenders and monitors

Dated evidence between site visits

Between monitoring visits, dated imagery shows where land clearing, construction, settlement around the site or resettlement villages have moved on, so the next visit goes to the places that changed. For a single grievance or claim, a location check puts every dated image that covers the point on one sheet, so your team can see what was there on each date. It supports an investigation; it does not decide the claim, and it does not replace the monitoring your lenders or regulators require.

How it works

From project area to reviewed baseline

  1. Scope

    You send the footprint or right of way, the state and LGA, the date the record must reflect and the deliverables your study needs. We agree the layers, the imagery and the format in a written proposal.

  2. Find the imagery

    We search the archive for dated scenes around the date that matters, and request a new capture where the archive is too old.

  3. Map and review

    Structures and land cover are mapped, and a person reviews every result. Drone detail is added where needed, subject to the NCAA and ONSA authorisations each job requires.

  4. Deliver

    GIS layers in your coordinate system, maps and a PDF report, then re-surveys after the cut-off on the schedule you set.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Record the structures in a footprint on dated imagery, reviewed by a person
  • Deliver settlement, land-cover, terrain and flood-exposure baselines as GIS layers
  • Estimate households from structure counts, with the assumptions stated
  • Flag structures that appear after the cut-off date, with evidence packs that support legal and community processes

What we don’t do

  • Enumerate people, or run the census or the socio-economic survey
  • Value structures or decide who is owed compensation
  • Set the cut-off date or decide eligibility
  • Verify title, a certificate of occupancy or a survey plan

Frequently asked questions

Is your baseline a substitute for the census and asset inventory?

No. It is a dated record of the structures in the footprint, with imagery, coordinates and IDs, that supports your census and asset inventory under IFC Performance Standard 5 and your compensation enumeration. Field teams still enumerate people and assets, and compensation needs ground verification.

Does the imagery set the cut-off date?

No. The cut-off date comes from your resettlement process. Our dated record documents what was on the ground on the imagery dates around it, and re-surveys after it show which structures are new.

Do you value structures for compensation?

No. Valuation stays with your valuers and the authorities. The Land Use Act values buildings at replacement cost less depreciation (s.29(4)); we supply the dated inventory of which structures stood where, with reviewer categories such as main building, outbuilding or under construction, which the valuation starts from.

Is an onshore pipeline on the EIA Act's mandatory list?

Not as a named item. The Act’s mandatory list names offshore pipelines over 50 kilometres, oil and gas field development, processing and storage facilities, refineries and large product depots near homes. Screening for an onshore line goes through the 2021 EIA Procedures and the Federal Ministry of Environment; your consultant will confirm the category.

Can you work as a subcontractor to our ESIA or RAP team?

Yes. We supply structure baselines, estimated households, land-cover baselines and GIS layers for your own maps and reports, in the formats and coordinate reference system your team uses.

Can your evidence packs be used in legal proceedings?

Whether a court or tribunal accepts a pack is for your lawyers; it supports legal and community processes. File fingerprints and an independent timestamp show that the files existed at that time and have not changed since. They don’t prove how the imagery was captured.

How are household numbers produced?

As estimates, from reviewed structure counts and stated persons-per-household assumptions. Every report sets the assumptions out, so your team can replace them with the figures from your own socio-economic survey.

Send us the project area

The footprint or right of way as KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile or GeoPackage, the state and LGA, the date the record must reflect (a cut-off date, a survey date or a construction date) and the deliverables your study needs. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
